prompt: What is productive efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Producing a given output at the lowest attainable cost.

options.label: B
options.text: Producing the combination of goods most preferred by consumers regardless of cost.

options.label: C
options.text: Making every consumer better off at the same time.

options.label: D
options.text: Producing only goods that generate positive externalities.

explanation: Productive efficiency concerns how output is produced. It exists when no more output can be obtained from the available resources without using additional resources, and for a firm it is associated with production at minimum average cost.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.1 definitions of productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: What is allocative efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Allocating resources to the mix of goods consumers value most.

options.label: B
options.text: Every firm produces at the lowest possible average cost.

options.label: C
options.text: The economy produces the maximum possible quantity of every good.

options.label: D
options.text: Income is distributed equally among all consumers.

explanation: Allocative efficiency concerns what is produced. Resources are directed toward the goods and services consumers value most relative to their opportunity cost.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.1 definitions of productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes productive efficiency from allocative efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Productive: equal incomes; allocative: equal output shares.

options.label: B
options.text: Productive: the preferred output mix; allocative: least cost.

options.label: C
options.text: Productive: least cost; allocative: the preferred output mix.

options.label: D
options.text: Productive: normal profits; allocative: maximum total revenue.

explanation: Productive efficiency asks whether output is produced using the least resources. Allocative efficiency asks whether scarce resources are devoted to the outputs most valued by consumers.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.1 definitions of productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: For a firm, productive efficiency is achieved when it operates

options.label: A
options.text: At minimum average cost.

options.label: B
options.text: At maximum total revenue.

options.label: C
options.text: At maximum marginal revenue.

options.label: D
options.text: At minimum average revenue.

explanation: The firm is productively efficient when it produces at the lowest attainable average cost, so resources are not being wasted in producing its output.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: In a market with full information and no externalities, the standard condition for allocative efficiency is

options.label: A
options.text: Price equals average fixed cost.

options.label: B
options.text: Marginal revenue equals marginal cost.

options.label: C
options.text: Price equals marginal cost.

options.label: D
options.text: Average revenue equals average cost.

explanation: Price represents the marginal value consumers place on the last unit, while marginal cost represents the opportunity cost of producing it. Equality indicates the efficient output.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: On a production possibility curve, which position is consistent with productive efficiency for the economy?

options.label: A
options.text: Any point inside the curve.

options.label: B
options.text: Any point outside the curve.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the midpoint of the curve.

options.label: D
options.text: A point on the PPC boundary.

explanation: A point on the PPC uses available resources fully and efficiently. At a point inside the curve, more of at least one output could be produced without reducing the other.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis
graphDescription: Vertical axis: capital goods. Horizontal axis: consumer goods. Draw a bowed-out PPC with point A on the frontier, point B inside it and point C outside it. The question concerns which position is productively efficient.

prompt: An economy is producing at a point inside its production possibility curve. What can be concluded?

options.label: A
options.text: It must be allocatively efficient.

options.label: B
options.text: It is Pareto optimal.

options.label: C
options.text: It is dynamically efficient.

options.label: D
options.text: It is productively inefficient.

explanation: A point inside the PPC indicates that more output is feasible with the existing resource base. This is productive inefficiency.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Assume full information and no externalities. If the market price of the last unit is $12 and its marginal cost is also $12, which condition is satisfied?

options.label: A
options.text: The productive-efficiency condition.

options.label: B
options.text: The allocative-efficiency condition.

options.label: C
options.text: The dynamic-efficiency condition.

options.label: D
options.text: The revenue-maximisation condition.

explanation: Allocative efficiency is associated with P = MC when price reflects marginal benefit and there are no externalities.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Assume full information and no externalities. If price exceeds marginal cost at the current output, what does the standard allocative-efficiency rule suggest?

options.label: A
options.text: Less of the product should be produced.

options.label: B
options.text: Output is already allocatively efficient.

options.label: C
options.text: The firm must be productively inefficient.

options.label: D
options.text: More of the product should be produced.

explanation: When P > MC, the marginal value to consumers exceeds the opportunity cost of producing another unit. Increasing output can therefore raise welfare until P = MC.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Assume full information and no externalities. If marginal cost exceeds price at the current output, allocative efficiency would normally require

options.label: A
options.text: A reduction in output.

options.label: B
options.text: An increase in output.

options.label: C
options.text: No change in output.

options.label: D
options.text: A rise in average fixed cost.

explanation: When MC > P, the cost of the last unit exceeds the value consumers place on it. Reducing output moves the market toward P = MC.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: What is Pareto optimality?

options.label: A
options.text: No household has less income than another.

options.label: B
options.text: No firm can earn more than normal profit.

options.label: C
options.text: No one can gain without someone else losing.

options.label: D
options.text: No consumer pays above the average production cost.

explanation: Pareto optimality is reached when every possible Pareto improvement has been exhausted: helping one person further would necessarily harm someone else.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.3 Pareto optimality | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: What is a Pareto improvement?

options.label: A
options.text: A change that raises total output even if every consumer is worse off.

options.label: B
options.text: At least one person becomes better off and no one becomes worse off.

options.label: C
options.text: A change that makes income distribution more equal.

options.label: D
options.text: A change that lowers the price of every product.

explanation: A Pareto improvement raises at least one person's welfare while leaving everyone else no worse off.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.3 Pareto optimality | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Why is a point inside an economy's PPC usually Pareto inefficient?

options.label: A
options.text: One output can rise without reducing the other.

options.label: B
options.text: All resources are already fully employed.

options.label: C
options.text: Moving to the PPC must make every person worse off.

options.label: D
options.text: The opportunity cost of every good is zero on the PPC.

explanation: Inside the PPC there are unused or inefficiently used resources. It is possible to increase at least one output without sacrificing the other, providing scope for a Pareto improvement.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.3 Pareto optimality | AO2 Analysis
graphDescription: Vertical axis: good Y. Horizontal axis: good X. Draw a PPC with point U inside and point E on the frontier northeast of U. Show that moving from U to E can increase one or both outputs without reducing the other.

graphScenes.caption: Schematic; labeled numbers specify quantitative values.

prompt: Which change is definitely a Pareto improvement?

options.label: A
options.text: National income rises but one household loses.

options.label: B
options.text: Consumer surplus rises but producer surplus falls.

options.label: C
options.text: One household gains while all others are unaffected.

options.label: D
options.text: Pollution falls but nearby households lose other benefits.

explanation: The definition requires at least one person to gain and nobody to lose. Aggregate gains alone are not sufficient.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.3 Pareto optimality | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Pareto optimality does not necessarily imply

options.label: A
options.text: That further Pareto improvements are impossible.

options.label: B
options.text: That making one person better off may require making another worse off.

options.label: C
options.text: An equal or equitable distribution of income.

options.label: D
options.text: That the allocation is Pareto efficient.

explanation: Pareto efficiency is about whether mutually non-harming improvements remain. It does not judge whether the distribution of income or wealth is fair.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.3 Pareto optimality | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: What is dynamic efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Producing at the lowest current average cost only.

options.label: B
options.text: Long-run efficiency gains from innovation and investment.

options.label: C
options.text: Producing where price equals marginal cost at a single point in time.

options.label: D
options.text: Making every individual better off simultaneously.

explanation: Dynamic efficiency is a longer-run concept. It reflects improvements over time through new products, new processes, research, development and investment.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.4 definition of dynamic efficiency | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which action is most likely to improve dynamic efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Keeping the existing production process unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: Raising price without changing costs or quality.

options.label: C
options.text: Producing at a point inside the PPC.

options.label: D
options.text: R&D that creates a lower-cost production process.

explanation: Dynamic efficiency comes from innovation and investment that improve productivity, products or production processes over time.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.4 definition of dynamic efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A firm replaces an old production line with automated equipment that lowers long-run unit costs. Which type of efficiency is most directly improved over time?

options.label: A
options.text: Allocative efficiency.

options.label: B
options.text: Pareto inefficiency.

options.label: C
options.text: Productive inefficiency.

options.label: D
options.text: Dynamic efficiency.

explanation: Investment in technology that lowers costs over time is a classic source of dynamic efficiency.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.4 definition of dynamic efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement about dynamic efficiency is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Current spending can buy future efficiency gains.

options.label: B
options.text: It can be judged only by whether P = MC today.

options.label: C
options.text: It requires a firm to avoid all investment expenditure.

options.label: D
options.text: It is identical to Pareto optimality.

explanation: Dynamic efficiency has an intertemporal dimension. Research and investment can raise present costs while producing future productivity gains or product improvements.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.4 definition of dynamic efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A firm's long-run average cost curve shifts downward after successful innovation. This is evidence of

options.label: A
options.text: Allocative inefficiency.

options.label: B
options.text: Dynamic efficiency.

options.label: C
options.text: Productive inefficiency.

options.label: D
options.text: Pareto inefficiency.

explanation: A downward shift in long-run average cost after innovation indicates that the firm can produce at lower cost over time, consistent with dynamic efficiency.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.4 definition of dynamic efficiency | AO2 Analysis
graphDescription: Vertical axis: cost per unit. Horizontal axis: output. Draw LRAC1 and a lower LRAC2 after innovation, with LRAC2 lying below LRAC1 over the relevant output range.

graphScenes.caption: Schematic; labeled numbers specify quantitative values.

prompt: What is market failure?

options.label: A
options.text: Any situation in which a firm earns a loss.

options.label: B
options.text: Any fall in the market price of a product.

options.label: C
options.text: Any government decision to regulate an industry.

options.label: D
options.text: Inefficient allocation by the free market.

explanation: Market failure exists when market forces left to themselves do not produce an efficient allocation of scarce resources.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.5 definition of market failure | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which outcome is an example of market failure?

options.label: A
options.text: Market share lost to a lower-cost rival.

options.label: B
options.text: Lower prices caused by increased market supply.

options.label: C
options.text: Under-consumption caused by underestimated personal benefits.

options.label: D
options.text: Consumer substitution toward a cheaper available product.

explanation: Under-provision caused by imperfect information means resources are not allocated to the socially desirable quantity and is therefore a form of market failure.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.5 definition of market failure | 7.3.6 reasons for market failure | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which is a reason why a free market may fail?

options.label: A
options.text: Social costs are included in private decisions.

options.label: B
options.text: Third-party effects are omitted from private decisions.

options.label: C
options.text: Consumers use complete and accurate product information.

options.label: D
options.text: Entry barriers are removed from formerly monopolised markets.

explanation: Externalities create a divergence between private and social costs or benefits, so the free-market outcome can be inefficient.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.6 reasons for market failure | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Why can public goods cause market failure?

options.label: A
options.text: Non-rivalry makes each consumer underestimate personal harm, so provision is excessive without government intervention.

options.label: B
options.text: Non-excludability removes the opportunity cost of production.

options.label: C
options.text: Non-rivalry requires provision by a single producer.

options.label: D
options.text: Non-excludability encourages free riding and weakens private financing.

explanation: Because non-payers cannot easily be excluded, private suppliers may be unable to collect enough revenue, causing under-provision or non-provision.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.6 reasons for market failure | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why can a merit good be under-consumed in a free market?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumers always know all benefits and costs.

options.label: B
options.text: Benefits are underestimated through imperfect information.

options.label: C
options.text: Its supply is necessarily perfectly elastic.

options.label: D
options.text: Its marginal cost is always zero.

explanation: A merit good may be under-consumed if consumers do not fully appreciate its benefits, producing an inefficient allocation of resources.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.6 reasons for market failure | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which market feature can lead to market failure through restricted output and higher prices?

options.label: A
options.text: Perfect information.

options.label: B
options.text: Abuse of monopoly power.

options.label: C
options.text: Free entry and exit.

options.label: D
options.text: A large number of price-taking firms.

explanation: A firm with substantial market power may restrict output below the allocatively efficient level, so price can exceed marginal cost.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.6 reasons for market failure | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which type of information problem can produce market failure?

options.label: A
options.text: Decisions made with incomplete or inaccurate information.

options.label: B
options.text: All market participants having identical and perfect information.

options.label: C
options.text: Every buyer knowing the full quality of every product.

options.label: D
options.text: Prices conveying complete information at zero cost.

explanation: Information failure can cause decisions that do not reflect true costs or benefits, leading to under- or over-allocation of resources.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.6 reasons for market failure | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which combination is required for economic efficiency in the textbook sense?

options.label: A
options.text: Dynamic efficiency and equal incomes.

options.label: B
options.text: Pareto optimality and zero profit only.

options.label: C
options.text: Maximum output and maximum prices.

options.label: D
options.text: Productive and allocative efficiency.

explanation: Economic efficiency requires resources to be used at least cost and allocated to the outputs most valued by consumers: productive plus allocative efficiency.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.1 definitions of productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Assume full information and no externalities. A firm produces at minimum average cost but price is above marginal cost. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is productively efficient but not allocatively efficient.

options.label: B
options.text: It is allocatively efficient but not productively efficient.

options.label: C
options.text: It is both productively and allocatively efficient.

options.label: D
options.text: It is neither productively nor allocatively efficient because minimum average cost is irrelevant.

explanation: Minimum average cost satisfies productive efficiency, while P > MC indicates that the market is producing less than the allocatively efficient quantity.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Assume full information and no externalities. A market produces where P = MC, but the firm's average cost is above its minimum. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The firm is productively efficient but the market is not allocatively efficient.

options.label: B
options.text: Allocatively efficient, but not productively efficient.

options.label: C
options.text: Both forms of efficiency are achieved.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither form can be assessed.

explanation: P = MC is the allocative condition. Productive efficiency additionally requires output at the minimum point of average cost.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis

Assume full information and no externalities. The table shows price and marginal cost for successive units of a product. At which quantity is allocative efficiency achieved?
| Quantity | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |

options.label: B
options.text: 3 units

options.label: C
options.text: 4 units

The table shows a firm's average costs. At which output is productive efficiency achieved?

options.label: A
options.text: 20 units

options.label: B
options.text: 30 units

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: 40 units

reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A firm is producing at output Q1 where average cost is falling as output rises. What does this imply?

options.label: A
options.text: The firm must already be allocatively efficient.

options.label: B
options.text: Productive efficiency has not yet been reached.

options.label: C
options.text: The firm is producing beyond minimum average cost.

options.label: D
options.text: The firm must be Pareto optimal.

explanation: If average cost is still falling, a larger output can be produced at a lower average cost. The minimum-average-cost condition for productive efficiency has not yet been reached.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A firm produces beyond the output at which average cost is minimum. Which change would move it toward productive efficiency, other things equal?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduce output toward minimum AC.

options.label: B
options.text: Increase output further beyond minimum AC.

options.label: C
options.text: Raise price toward maximum total revenue.

options.label: D
options.text: Reduce price toward average fixed cost.

explanation: On the rising section of AC, average cost is above its minimum. Moving output back toward minimum AC improves productive efficiency.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Assume full information and no externalities. At output Q, consumers are willing to pay $18 for the last unit while its marginal cost is $12. Which conclusion follows?

options.label: A
options.text: Resources are allocated excessively to this product.

options.label: B
options.text: Resources are allocated efficiently to this product.

options.label: C
options.text: Production necessarily occurs at minimum average cost.

options.label: D
options.text: Resources are allocated insufficiently to this product.

explanation: The marginal benefit represented by price exceeds marginal cost. Additional production would create more benefit than cost, so too few resources are currently allocated to the product.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Assume full information and no externalities. At output Q, marginal cost is $15 while consumers value the last unit at $9. Which conclusion follows?

options.label: A
options.text: There is under-allocation of resources to this product.

options.label: B
options.text: Allocative efficiency is achieved.

options.label: C
options.text: There is over-allocation of resources to this product.

options.label: D
options.text: Dynamic efficiency is necessarily achieved.

explanation: MC > P means the last unit costs more to produce than consumers value it. Resources should be released from this production until P = MC.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Assume full information and no externalities. The diagram shows a horizontal price line and an upward-sloping MC curve. Which output represents allocative efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: The smallest positive output.

options.label: B
options.text: The output where MC is zero.

options.label: C
options.text: The output where price intersects MC.

options.label: D
options.text: The output where the price line is furthest above MC.

explanation: Allocative efficiency occurs at the output where marginal willingness to pay, represented by price, equals marginal cost.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Assume full information and no externalities. A firm's AC curve reaches its minimum at Qp, while P = MC at a larger output Qa. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Productive efficiency at Qp; allocative efficiency at Qa.

options.label: B
options.text: Both efficiencies occur at Qp.

options.label: C
options.text: Both efficiencies occur at Qa.

options.label: D
options.text: Allocative efficiency occurs at Qp and productive efficiency at Qa.

explanation: The two efficiency conditions need not occur at the same output. Minimum AC identifies productive efficiency, while P = MC identifies allocative efficiency.

prompt: Why can a point on a PPC establish productive efficiency but not, by itself, allocative efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: The PPC does not reveal the preferred output mix.

options.label: B
options.text: The PPC contains no scarce resources.

options.label: C
options.text: Allocative efficiency requires a point inside the PPC.

options.label: D
options.text: Productive efficiency can occur only when P = MC.

explanation: Every point on the frontier can be productively efficient, but the socially preferred point depends on valuations and opportunity costs not contained in the PPC alone.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.1 definitions of productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Assume full information and no externalities. A market moves from P > MC to P = MC without changing the firm's average-cost position. What has definitely improved?

options.label: A
options.text: Productive efficiency.

options.label: B
options.text: Allocative efficiency.

options.label: C
options.text: Income equality.

options.label: D
options.text: Dynamic efficiency.

explanation: The movement to P = MC directly satisfies the allocative condition. Nothing in the information guarantees movement to minimum average cost or investment-driven improvements.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A market moves from an output above minimum average cost to the minimum of AC, while P remains above MC. What has definitely improved?

options.label: A
options.text: Allocative efficiency.

options.label: B
options.text: Productive efficiency.

options.label: C
options.text: Dynamic efficiency.

options.label: D
options.text: Income equality.

explanation: Moving to minimum AC reduces the resource cost of producing the output. P > MC still indicates allocative inefficiency.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: An economy moves from inside its PPC to the frontier, producing more of both goods. The additional goods are allocated without reducing anyone’s consumption or welfare, and no other welfare losses occur. At least one recipient is better off. How should this change be described?

options.label: A
options.text: A Pareto deterioration and allocative inefficiency.

options.label: B
options.text: A fall in productive efficiency.

options.label: C
options.text: A Pareto improvement with higher efficiency.

options.label: D
options.text: A change that must reduce dynamic efficiency.

explanation: Moving to the frontier improves productive efficiency. Under the stated distribution and welfare assumptions, some people benefit and no one loses, so it is also a Pareto improvement.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | 7.3.3 Pareto optimality | AO2 Analysis
graphDescription: Vertical axis: good Y. Horizontal axis: good X. Draw a PPC. Mark A inside the PPC and B on the PPC northeast of A so both X and Y are greater at B.

prompt: An economy moves along its PPC to produce more capital goods and fewer consumer goods. Is this necessarily a Pareto improvement?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes; more capital goods always increase current welfare.

options.label: B
options.text: No; some consumers may lose from the output change.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes; any change between frontier points improves everyone’s welfare.

options.label: D
options.text: No; every frontier point implies idle productive resources.

explanation: A movement along the frontier involves an opportunity cost. The gain in one output is accompanied by a loss of another, so some individuals may be worse off.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.3 Pareto optimality | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A policy creates benefits of $20 million for one group and losses of $5 million for another. What can be concluded using the strict Pareto criterion?

options.label: A
options.text: It is automatically a Pareto improvement because benefits exceed losses.

options.label: B
options.text: It is automatically Pareto optimal because net benefits are positive.

options.label: C
options.text: Not unless the losing group is no worse off.

options.label: D
options.text: It must reduce productive efficiency.

explanation: The Pareto criterion does not aggregate gains and losses. Any uncompensated loser prevents the change from being a Pareto improvement.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.3 Pareto optimality | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A road project reduces travel times for most residents but increases noise for households near the road. Why is the project not automatically a Pareto improvement?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduced travel time has no opportunity-cost value.

options.label: B
options.text: New infrastructure necessarily raises average production costs.

options.label: C
options.text: Nearby households may lose welfare through additional noise.

options.label: D
options.text: Pareto improvements require equal incomes between all households.

prompt: With full information and no externalities, a market produces where P = MC and firms operate at minimum average cost. What do these conditions establish?

options.label: A
options.text: Static efficiency and evidence of continuing product innovation.

options.label: B
options.text: Static efficiency without evidence of continuing product innovation.

options.label: C
options.text: Equal income distribution and evidence of continuing product innovation.

options.label: D
options.text: Equal income distribution without evidence of continuing product innovation.

explanation: P = MC establishes allocative efficiency under the stated assumptions; minimum average cost establishes productive efficiency. These static conditions do not establish innovation over time or an equitable income distribution.

prompt: Assume full information and no externalities. The graph shows a market output Qm where P > MC and an efficient output Qe where P = MC. What is the most direct interpretation of Qm?

options.label: A
options.text: Resources are allocated excessively to this product.

options.label: B
options.text: Production necessarily occurs at minimum average cost.

options.label: C
options.text: The output necessarily maximises future innovation gains.

options.label: D
options.text: Resources are allocated insufficiently to this product.

explanation: At Qm, consumers value extra output more than it costs to produce. Expanding toward Qe can increase welfare, so the market under-allocates resources to the product.

prompt: Assume full information and no externalities. The graph shows output Qx where MC > P and a lower output Qe where P = MC. What is the most direct interpretation of Qx?

options.label: D

prompt: A market outcome satisfies P = private MC, but consumers have seriously underestimated the benefits of a merit good. Which conclusion is best?

options.label: A
options.text: Allocative inefficiency may remain because informed demand is higher.

options.label: B
options.text: P = private MC proves the allocation is socially efficient in all circumstances.

options.label: C
options.text: The market is productively inefficient by definition.

options.label: D
options.text: The good must be a public good.

explanation: If consumers underestimate benefits, observed willingness to pay does not reflect fully informed valuation. The simple private P = MC condition can therefore be misleading.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | 7.3.6 reasons for market failure | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A market outcome satisfies P = private MC, but production imposes external costs. Which conclusion is best?

options.label: A
options.text: P = private MC guarantees social allocative efficiency.

options.label: B
options.text: External costs imply the product is necessarily a public good.

options.label: C
options.text: Private MC omits third-party costs, so output may be excessive.

options.label: D
options.text: The market must be productively inefficient.

explanation: The standard P = MC condition relies on private and social costs coinciding. External costs break that link, so the private-market output can be excessive.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | 7.3.6 reasons for market failure | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which change can improve productive efficiency without changing allocative efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: The market expands output from P > MC to P = MC with no cost change.

options.label: B
options.text: Consumers receive better information and demand shifts to the informed level.

options.label: C
options.text: A public good becomes non-excludable.

options.label: D
options.text: A lower-cost production method with unchanged output and P relative to MC.

explanation: Lowering the resource cost of producing the existing output improves productive efficiency. If the relationship between price and marginal cost at the market output is unchanged, allocative efficiency need not change.

prompt: Assume full information and no externalities. Which change can improve allocative efficiency without improving productive efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: The firm moves to minimum AC while P stays above MC.

options.label: B
options.text: The firm innovates and shifts LRAC downward while output remains restricted.

options.label: C
options.text: The economy moves from an inside-PPC point to the frontier with the same output mix.

options.label: D
options.text: Market output moves to P = MC while the firm remains above minimum average cost.

explanation: Moving to P = MC corrects the marginal allocation even if the firm still produces at an unnecessarily high average cost.
reference: 7.3 Efficiency and market failure | 7.3.2 conditions for productive efficiency and allocative efficiency | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which change can improve dynamic efficiency while worsening current productive efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Eliminating current production waste without introducing any innovation.

options.label: B
options.text: Moving to the minimum of the existing AC curve.

options.label: C
options.text: Accepting higher current costs to develop cheaper future methods.

options.label: D
options.text: Moving output toward the current P = MC intersection.

explanation: Research spending can raise current average cost while creating innovations that shift future costs downward. Dynamic efficiency therefore can conflict with static productive efficiency in the short run.

prompt: A policy makes an economy more allocatively efficient but reduces the income of one group. Which statement follows?

options.label: A
options.text: Allocative efficiency can rise without a Pareto improvement.

options.label: B
options.text: The policy must be a Pareto improvement because efficiency rises.

options.label: C
options.text: Allocative efficiency and Pareto improvement are identical concepts.

options.label: D
options.text: The income loss proves productive inefficiency.

explanation: Efficiency gains can create losers. Pareto improvement applies a separate no-one-worse-off criterion.

prompt: A technological innovation lowers costs for a firm but destroys demand for workers with specialised skills. Which conclusion about Pareto improvement is best?

options.label: A
options.text: Cost reductions guarantee that every affected household gains welfare.

options.label: B
options.text: Innovation guarantees that all displaced workers find equivalent jobs.

options.label: C
options.text: Displaced workers may lose despite benefits to the innovating firm.

options.label: D
options.text: Reduced employment rules out any efficiency gains from the innovation.

explanation: Dynamic efficiency can rise while some people lose. The strict Pareto criterion therefore cannot be inferred from a productivity gain alone.

prompt: A product is under-provided because it is non-excludable, and consumers also underestimate its wider benefits. Which conclusion is best?

options.label: A
options.text: Free riding is the only possible source of under-provision.

options.label: B
options.text: Information failure necessarily increases output enough to remove free riding.

options.label: C
options.text: Free riding and underestimated benefits offset each other exactly.

options.label: D
options.text: Free riding and underestimated benefits can both reinforce under-allocation.

explanation: Non-excludability weakens private provision, while underestimated benefits depress demand. Both mechanisms can push the market quantity below the socially desirable level.

prompt: Assume full information and no externalities. A regulator observes that P = MC and AC is at its minimum after intervention. Which statement is still not guaranteed?

options.label: A
options.text: The firm is productively efficient at that output.

options.label: B
options.text: The market is dynamically efficient over time.

options.label: C
options.text: The standard allocative-efficiency condition is met.

options.label: D
options.text: Both static efficiency conditions are satisfied.

explanation: The observed conditions establish current productive and allocative efficiency in the model, but they reveal nothing about innovation, investment or future cost reduction.

prompt: Which statement best summarises why efficiency analysis is central to market failure?

options.label: A
options.text: Market failure is identified whenever prices change.

options.label: B
options.text: Market failure is identified whenever firms innovate.

options.label: C
options.text: Market failure is identical to an unequal income distribution.

options.label: D
options.text: Compare the market outcome with an efficient benchmark.

explanation: The concept of market failure is meaningful only relative to an efficiency benchmark: resources are either wasted, misallocated, or both.
